channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Novel platform reveals new metabolic targets for cancer treatment
item.description: Cancer cells are hungry beasts. To fuel growth and division, tumors rewire a cell's metabolism, diverting nutrients into the energy and raw materials they need to survive. But not all cancers have the same metabolic needs, and a new study reveals how different cancer-causing mutations can shape metabolism even within the same organ.

item.title: An engineered 'glue' for aged eggs could prevent premature chromosome separation
Oral nutrition supplement interventions show short-term benefits in patient outcomes at low cost for older adults
item.description: A systematic review published in the journal Value in Health by Amarsinh Desai, Ph.D., Olivia M. Dong, Ph.D., and colleagues examines the health and economic effects of oral nutrition supplements in older adults, most with or at risk of malnutrition. The researchers found that oral nutrition supplement use, often as part of broader nutrition interventions, was generally associated with modest short-term improvements in health outcomes and was cost-effective or cost-saving, with economic benefits largely driven by reductions in health care resource utilization, such as fewer hospitalizations.

item.title: A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer
item.description: Cancer begins in DNA, which is why everything about this well-known molecule is extensively studied at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO). For instance, what exactly happens when DNA is duplicated? Every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, its DNA is copied. Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have now uncovered a new aspect of this complex process, which has been studied for decades but still holds many surprises.

item.title: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia
item.description: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that an experimental drug may help overcome one of the major challenges in treating an aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), known as FLT3-positive AML. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI-101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.

item.title: A forgotten organ sheds new light on the origins of the ovary
item.description: How do ovaries develop? Much remains unknown. By studying the "rete ovarii," a small anatomical structure that has long been overlooked, a team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) has uncovered the dual origin of the cells that surround and protect oocytes. This discovery offers new insights into ovarian development and opens up new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.

item.title: New evidence suggests heart cells transmit electrical signals through more than direct connections
item.description: Your heart may beat 3 billion times or more over a long lifetime. Across 75 years or longer, it carries on without a thought while you sleep, work and exercise.

item.title: Brain immune cells could weaken motor memories by removing myelin, study suggests
item.description: When people and other mammals learn new movements, connections between some of their brain cells become stronger. Yet studies have shown that learning motor skills also prompts changes in myelin, an insulating material around nerve fibers produced by cells called oligodendrocytes.

item.title: Form and diversity: How tumor architecture shapes colorectal cancer progression
item.description: Tumors are not uniform, as even cancer cells within one patient can display extremely divergent characteristics and behaviors. This diversity, known as tumor heterogeneity, reduces therapeutic efficacy because cells in different states may respond differently to therapeutic interventions.

item.title: Stronger molecular grip optimizes anticancer drug release
item.description: Researchers from Osaka Metropolitan University have modified a naturally occurring protein so that it can hold on to an anticancer drug more tightly, potentially preventing the drug from being released before it reaches its intended destination.

item.title: Risk for disease flare low for women with IBD undergoing assisted reproductive technology
item.description: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART) have low flare rates and live birth rates comparable to those of the general population, according to a study published online Nov. 10 in Inflammatory Bowel Diseases.

item.title: 'It's scary': California battles West Nile virus surge
item.description: For two months, Mandi Budd has been unable to use her legs—she is paralyzed because of a mosquito bite that nearly took her life.

item.title: The same gene that helps define neuron identity may also balance developing brain circuits
item.description: A gene that helps set a neuron's identity also affects how many inputs it receives from other neurons. New research led by neuroscientists at King's College London finds that the molecules neurons use to wire together in the developing mouse brain depend on the role these neurons will play in the adult. The connections these neurons form also depend on how electrically active they are during development.

item.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo reaches 12,000 cases as violence forces some responders to evacuate
item.description: The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

item.title: 2000 to 2024 saw decrease in age-adjusted stroke death rate in U.S.
item.description: During 2000 to 2024, there was a decrease in the age-adjusted stroke death rate, although rates increased among certain groups in the most recent trend periods, according to research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

item.title: One body, two systems: Integrating dental and medical care dramatically improves dental follow-up
Electronic health record algorithm can identify drug-resistant epilepsy
item.description: An electronic health record (EHR) algorithm can identify people with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), according to a study published in the December issue of Epilepsy & Behavior.

item.title: Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors
item.description: For lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue, a multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue, and the effect is maintained to six months, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

item.title: Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later
item.description: Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.

item.title: Ecuadorian plant shows potential to control bacteria in food
item.description: A plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador could have a new application: helping control bacteria in ready-to-eat foods. A study published in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto food model.

item.title: Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively
item.description: A recent study in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored how researchers can better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions designed to improve dietary habits and reduce cardiovascular risk.

item.title: Premature screen use can take away play, movement, and face-to-face interaction from young children
item.description: Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by the age of 18 months, yet what they need most for their development is play, physical activity, face-to-face interactions and active exploration of their surroundings. Early and intensive use of digital devices may pose risks not only because of the time spent in front of screens, but also because it may take time away from these essential experiences.

item.title: How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk
item.description: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. Most firearm owners prioritize safety, research shows, but strategies aimed at firearm injury prevention among youth have largely focused on policy change instead of teaching them how to identify injury risk.

item.title: Dad's antidepressant use linked to higher metabolic disorder risk in children
item.description: Use of antidepressants by fathers in the months just before pregnancy is associated with a slightly increased risk of metabolic disorders, particularly high blood pressure, in their children, finds a large study from Denmark published by The BMJ.

item.title: ADHD meds in pregnancy not linked to developmental disorders in children
item.description: Children born to mothers who used attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medication during pregnancy face no increased risk of neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, ADHD, intellectual disability and learning disorders, finds a large Scandinavian study published by The BMJ.

item.title: Gut microbiome may shape blood sugar benefits of whole grains
item.description: People with prediabetes are at very high risk for developing type 2 diabetes, and improving their diet is one way they can try to fend off advanced disease.

item.title: Heart failure: Advances include earlier detection, treatment options, expert explains
item.description: Heart failure is a common complication of heart conditions; collectively, cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death globally. In heart failure, the heart doesn't pump blood well enough to meet the body's needs, causing a range of symptoms. Jose Nativi Nicolau, M.D., a transplant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic in Florida, describes advances in detection and treatment.

item.title: Genetic information can improve prostate cancer risk assessment
item.description: Genetic information can help provide a more individual assessment of prostate cancer risk among men undergoing PSA testing, according to a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in JAMA Network Open. PSA is a protein produced by the prostate that can be measured with a blood test. An elevated PSA level can be a sign of prostate cancer, but PSA levels can also be affected by other changes in the prostate.

item.title: Membrane developed for dry eye treatment can improve symptoms
item.description: A study led by Aston University's Travé Huarte has shown that a new single six-day treatment for moderate to severe dry eye disease using a modified, windowed amniotic membrane can deliver sustained symptom relief with good treatment compliance.

item.title: Preclinical study suggests corin may help treat deadly brain tumor in infants
item.description: A drug called corin might help treat the most common form of brain cancer in infants, according to a study by Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers. Corin, which was developed at Johns Hopkins Medicine, causes tumor cells to mature into a less aggressive state.
